node-1.label: After three months of therapy, the patient experienced two days of nausea, vomiting, and subjective fevers

node-2.label: Patient is a 29-year-old woman from the Dominican Republic who moved to the United States in 2014; presented in January 2016 for prenatal care; PPD skin test was positive (21 mm).

node-3.label: In January 2022, she was started on rifampin 300 mg daily for a planned 4-month course; she was taking no other medications.

node-4.label: Initial physical examination showed no significant physical examination findings noted in the case report.

why.why: The patient was still taking rifampin when the nausea, vomiting, fever, and abnormal laboratory results developed, and rifampin is a recognized cause of immune hemolytic anemia and thrombotic microangiopathy. The laboratory expert strongly supports rifampin adverse effect, so confidence is increased from 0.92 to 0.93. Confirmatory tests remain pending for the specific syndrome, but the broad adverse drug effect is well supported.

The patient was still taking rifampin when the syndrome developed, and the laboratory expert explicitly interprets the hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury pattern as inconsistent with infection. Ongoing rifampin therapy also makes active TB unlikely, so confidence is decreased from 0.05 to 0.04.

The systemic pattern of hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury occurring during rifampin treatment points strongly to drug toxicity rather than a non-drug gastrointestinal cause. The laboratory expert also regards GI causes as inconsistent, reducing confidence from 0.03 to 0.02.

node-8.label: Laboratory tests show acute kidney injury with creatinine 3.8 mg/dL

node-9.label: Laboratory tests show thrombocytopenia with platelet count 84 K/μL

node-10.label: Laboratory tests show hemolysis with haptoglobin <10 mg/dL and LDH 1125 U/L

node-11.label: Laboratory tests show elevated AST, proteinuria, and hematuria

node-13.label: Rifampin-induced immune hemolytic anemia/thrombotic microangiopathy with acute kidney injury

why.why: The characteristic combination of acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, elevated AST, proteinuria, and hematuria with normal baseline values, occurring during ongoing rifampin therapy, is strongly supported by the laboratory expert as rifampin-induced immune hemolytic anemia/thrombotic microangiopathy with acute kidney injury. However, peripheral smear, Coombs, ADAMTS13, and rifampin antibody results remain unavailable, so definitive confirmation is pending; confidence remains 0.85.
